topics.title: Extratropical cyclone life cycle
lesson: Mid-latitude lows form along the polar front where warm and cold air meet. The classic Norwegian (Bjerknes) model describes their life cycle.

list: 1. Initial disturbance: a small wave on a stationary front.
2. Open wave: warm sector develops between a warm front ahead and a cold front behind. Pressure falls and winds increase.
3. Deepening: the cold front moves faster than the warm front and closes on it. The warm sector narrows.
4. Occlusion: the cold front overtakes the warm front. The low is usually at or near its greatest intensity around this time.
5. Dissipation: the warm air is cut off from the surface, the low fills and weakens. The cyclone becomes cold-cored.

lesson: Surface cyclogenesis needs upper-level support. A shortwave trough aloft with divergence ahead of it, positive vorticity advection, and a strong temperature gradient (baroclinic zone) all help. The surface low deepens when upper-level divergence exceeds surface convergence.

Explosive cyclogenesis (a weather bomb) is a fall in central pressure of at least 24 hPa in 24 hours at 60 N, scaled by sin(latitude) at other latitudes. These storms are common off the east coast of North America in winter and are major hazards for Atlantic Canada and the North Atlantic.

lesson.note: Typical life span: a few days. Surface lows generally move in the direction of the 500 hPa flow above them.

terms: Cyclogenesis
Development or intensification of a low-pressure system.
Warm sector
Region of warm air between the cold and warm fronts of a cyclone.
Explosive cyclogenesis
Rapid deepening of at least 24 hPa in 24 h (at 60 N).

questions.q: When does an extratropical cyclone typically reach its greatest intensity?
c: Around the time of occlusion
At its first appearance as a frontal wave
After it has fully dissipated
When the warm sector is widest
questions.e: Maximum deepening is usually near the start of occlusion, after which the system gradually weakens.

questions.q: What is the general criterion for a 'bomb' cyclone?
c: Central pressure falls 24 hPa or more in 24 hours (at 60 N)
Central pressure rises 24 hPa or more in 24 hours at any latitude
Sustained winds reach 120 km/h within the first 24 hours of life
The cold front travels faster than 24 km/h for 24 hours
questions.e: The criterion is a 24 hPa fall in 24 hours at 60 N, scaled for other latitudes.

questions.q: Which upper-air feature typically supports surface cyclogenesis?
c: A trough aloft with divergence ahead of it
A ridge aloft
A cut-off high
Uniform zonal flow with no gradient
questions.e: Upper divergence removes mass from the column and lowers surface pressure.

questions.q: In a developing cyclone, the warm sector lies between:
c: The warm front and the cold front
Two warm fronts
Two cold fronts
The low centre and the high centre
questions.e: The warm sector is the wedge of warm air between the two fronts.

questions.q: In the dissipation stage, an extratropical cyclone:
c: Fills and becomes cold-cored
Strengthens rapidly
Becomes a tropical cyclone
Develops a warm core
questions.e: Warm air is cut off from the surface and the low fills.

questions.q: Which stage of the cyclone life cycle is marked by the lowest central pressure?
c: Occluded (mature) stage
Initial wave stage
Incipient stage
Dissipating after fully filled
questions.e: Maximum intensity commonly occurs near the time of occlusion.

questions.q: The Norwegian cyclone model begins with a wave on a:
c: Stationary front
Warm sector high
Dry line
Tropical wave
questions.e: A small wave on a quasi-stationary polar front starts cyclogenesis.

questions.q: A deepening cyclone means central pressure:
c: Is falling
Is rising
Is steady
Is the same as the high
questions.e: Deepening means the central pressure decreases.

questions.q: Rapid cyclogenesis, often called a bomb, is a pressure fall of about:
c: 24 hPa in 24 hours at 60 degrees latitude
1 hPa in 24 hours at any latitude, however slowly it moves
5 hPa in 24 hours, as measured near the centre of the low
100 hPa in 24 hours, a value seen only in tropical storms
questions.e: Bombogenesis is defined as about 24 hPa in 24 h at 60 N, scaled by latitude.

questions.q: Cyclones in the Atlantic region tend to move generally toward the:
c: Northeast
Southwest
South
West
questions.e: Mid-latitude storm tracks run west to east, often toward the northeast along the coast.

questions.q: The surface low is located relative to the upper trough as it develops. Strengthening occurs when the upper trough is:
c: West of the surface low (tilting back with height)
Directly over the surface low, with no tilt in the vertical
East of the surface low, tilting forward with height
Absent altogether, since development is driven only at the surface
questions.e: A westward tilt with height allows upper divergence to exceed surface convergence.

topics.title: Upper-air patterns (troughs, ridges, cut-off lows)
lesson: The mid-latitude flow aloft is a wavy pattern of troughs and ridges called Rossby waves. They steer surface systems.

list: Trough: elongated area of low heights with cyclonic curvature. Cold air, rising motion ahead of the axis, cloud and precipitation.
Ridge: elongated area of high heights with anticyclonic curvature. Warm air, sinking motion, fair weather.
Long waves: 3 to 6 around the hemisphere, slow-moving, set the large-scale pattern.
Short waves: smaller disturbances embedded in the flow, moving quickly with the wind. Each one can trigger surface development.
Zonal: mostly west to east. Fast-moving systems, mild changes.
Meridional: large north-south swings. Cold outbreaks and warm surges. Systems can slow down.
Cut-off low: a closed low that separates from the main westerlies. Slow-moving, can persist for days, with cold air aloft, showers and unsettled weather.
Blocking high (for example an omega block): a strong ridge that stalls the flow. Storms are diverted around it and the same weather can persist for a week or more.

lesson: At 500 hPa the flow is parallel to the height contours with low heights on the left (Northern Hemisphere). Closer contours mean stronger winds.

lesson.note: Surface lows tend to track on the downstream side of troughs and beneath the jet axis.

terms: Rossby wave
Large-scale wave in the mid-latitude westerlies.
Cut-off low
Closed upper low isolated from the main flow.
Blocking
A persistent, strong ridge that stalls the normal west-to-east motion.

questions.q: What characterizes a cut-off low?
c: A slow-moving closed low detached from the westerly flow, often with persistent unsettled weather
A fast-moving ridge embedded in the westerlies that brings short spells of clear weather
A weak surface high that stays over the same area and brings steady clear skies
A stationary front at the surface that separates two air masses for several days
questions.e: Cut-off lows can linger for days, bringing cold air aloft and showers.

questions.q: What conditions go with an upper-level ridge?
c: Warm air, sinking motion, fair weather
Cold air, strong ascent, heavy rain
Strong jet streaks only
Tropical cyclones
questions.e: Ridges are associated with anticyclonic curvature, subsidence and mostly dry weather.

questions.q: At 500 hPa in the Northern Hemisphere, flow is parallel to height contours with:
c: Lower heights on the left
Lower heights on the right
Higher heights on the left
Contours crossing at right angles
questions.e: Near-geostrophic flow keeps low heights on the left.

questions.q: What is a blocking pattern?
c: A persistent strong ridge that stalls the west-to-east flow
A mountain range that blocks surface winds and causes rain shadows
A cold front that has stalled for more than a day over one region
A strong jet stream that moves faster than the surface storms below
questions.e: Blocks divert storms and can lock in the same weather for long periods.

questions.q: Long waves in the westerlies typically number:
c: 3 to 6 around the hemisphere
20 to 30 around the hemisphere
Exactly 12 around the hemisphere
Only one wave around the hemisphere
questions.e: Planetary-scale Rossby waves are few, large and slow.

questions.q: A ridge in the upper flow is generally associated with:
c: Warm air, fair weather and subsidence
Cold air and storms
Frontogenesis and heavy rain
Strong convergence at the surface
questions.e: Ridges support high pressure and drier, sinking air.

questions.q: A cut-off low is:
c: A closed low separated from the main westerlies
A low that moves rapidly along with the main jet stream
A surface low that has moved out over the open water
A trough that leads a ridge by about a thousand kilometres
questions.e: Cut-off lows detach from the flow and may stay in place for days.

questions.q: A Rex block comprises:
c: A high poleward of a low
A low poleward of a high
Two highs side by side
A single trough
questions.e: A Rex block has a high to the north and a low to the south.

questions.q: At 500 hPa, a short-wave trough is best described as:
c: A small-scale disturbance moving quickly in the flow
A stationary planetary-scale wave that changes very slowly
A surface boundary separating two different air masses
A tropical wave moving westward in the trade wind flow
questions.e: Short waves move quickly and trigger local development.

questions.q: What does an omega block look like?
c: A high flanked by lows, resembling the Greek letter
A single deep trough with a strong jet stream on its east side
A jet streak with divergence on its left exit region
A line of thunderstorms curving around a surface low
questions.e: The ridge with troughs on both sides resembles the Greek letter omega.

questions.q: Weather beneath a persistent upper ridge often includes:
c: Dry, stable weather and possible heat or poor air quality
Heavy continuous snow with rapid temperature drops and gales
A steady stream of fast-moving lows with fronts every day
Frequent tornadoes and severe thunderstorms across the region
questions.e: Persistent ridges suppress cloud and allow heating.

topics.title: Vorticity and divergence
lesson: Vorticity measures local spin. Divergence measures horizontal spreading of air. They link upper-air patterns to surface weather.

list: Relative vorticity: spin relative to the Earth. Positive means cyclonic (counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere).
Planetary vorticity (f): spin due to Earth's rotation, greater toward the poles.
Absolute vorticity = relative + planetary. It is roughly conserved in large-scale flow.
Relative vorticity maxima occur in the base of troughs (curvature) and in cyclonic shear zones on the left side of a jet.

Positive vorticity advection (PVA): higher vorticity moves in. At mid-levels (500 hPa) this is associated with upper divergence and rising motion, which favours cloud, precipitation, and falling surface pressure.
Negative vorticity advection (NVA): associated with sinking motion and clearing.

lesson: Divergence aloft must be balanced by upward motion beneath it, which draws in air at lower levels (convergence). If upper divergence exceeds surface convergence, surface pressure falls and a low deepens.

lesson.note: Stack to remember: upper divergence over surface convergence equals rising air and a developing low.

terms: Vorticity
Measure of local rotation in a fluid.
PVA
Positive vorticity advection: movement of higher vorticity air into an area.
Mass continuity
Principle that air removed by divergence must be replaced by vertical motion and convergence.

questions.q: What does positive relative vorticity represent in the Northern Hemisphere?
c: Cyclonic (counterclockwise) rotation
Anticyclonic (clockwise) rotation
No rotation
Strong sinking
questions.e: Positive vorticity is counterclockwise spin in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: What does PVA at 500 hPa usually indicate?
c: Rising motion that favours cloud and falling surface pressure
Sinking motion that favours clearing and rising surface pressure
A stationary front with no vertical motion near the 500 hPa level
Calm winds at all levels with no change in vertical motion
questions.e: PVA is linked to upper divergence and ascent.

questions.q: Where are relative vorticity maxima typically found?
c: In the base of troughs and in cyclonic shear zones
At the crests of ridges and in anticyclonic shear zones
In the stratosphere above the tropopause over the poles
Over warm oceans where the sea surface is warmest
questions.e: Trough curvature and cyclonic shear both add positive vorticity.

questions.q: Divergence aloft over a surface low generally causes:
c: Surface pressure to fall
Surface pressure to rise
No change in pressure
The low to vanish at once
questions.e: Mass is removed from the column, lowering pressure at the surface.

questions.q: NVA at mid-levels is generally linked to:
c: Sinking motion and clearing
Rising motion and heavier cloud
Rapid deepening of a surface low
Strong convergence and falling pressure
questions.e: Negative vorticity advection favours subsidence.

questions.q: Positive vorticity advection (PVA) typically leads to:
c: Upward motion and falling surface pressure
Subsidence, clearing skies and rising surface pressure
No vertical motion, since vorticity does not affect vertical motion
Rapid dissipation of the trough and the end of the system
questions.e: PVA ahead of a trough enhances upward motion.

questions.q: The flow ahead of an upper trough tends to show:
c: Divergence aloft and rising motion
Convergence aloft and sinking motion
No divergence
Uniform vorticity
questions.e: East of the trough axis, divergence aloft supports ascent.

questions.q: Cyclonic vorticity in the Northern Hemisphere has a rotation sense of:
c: Counterclockwise
Clockwise
No rotation
Variable
questions.e: Cyclonic is counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: Upper-level divergence is stronger than low-level convergence. Surface pressure will:
c: Fall
Rise
Remain steady
Oscillate
questions.e: Net mass removal from the column lowers surface pressure.

questions.q: Where is vorticity maximum typically found?
c: At the base of a trough
At the crest of a ridge
In the middle of a high
At the equator
questions.e: Curvature vorticity peaks at the trough axis.

questions.q: In quasi-geostrophic thinking, ascent is forced by:
c: Differential vorticity advection and temperature advection
Surface friction acting on the lower layers of the atmosphere only
Radiative cooling of the upper troposphere at night alone
Pure orographic lift with no link to upper-level flow
questions.e: QG omega depends on vorticity advection change with height and thermal advection.

topics.title: Mesoscale systems (MCS, squall lines)
lesson: Mesoscale systems range from a few km to several hundred km and last from hours to a day. They are often missed by global models and need radar and satellite to monitor.

list: Mesoscale convective system (MCS): an organized cluster of thunderstorms that acts as one system, often with a large anvil and stratiform rain area.
Mesoscale convective complex (MCC): a large, nearly circular MCS identified from cold cloud tops on infrared imagery. Often forms in the evening and lasts into the night.
Squall line: a line of thunderstorms with a continuous gust front, often marked by a shelf cloud, sudden wind shift, temperature drop and heavy rain.
Bow echo: radar signature of a bowed line of storms producing damaging straight-line winds.
Derecho: a widespread, long-lived windstorm moving across a large area (hundreds of km) with a swath of damaging straight-line winds.
Gust front: leading edge of cold outflow from thunderstorms. It can arrive well before the rain.
Sea breeze front and lake breeze fronts: focus convection.
Lake-effect snow: cold air crossing relatively warm open lake water becomes unstable and produces intense snow bands on the downwind shore.
Polar lows: small, intense maritime lows in cold air outbreaks over open ocean.

lesson.note: In Atlantic Canada, mesoscale bands in winter storms can produce snowfall rates far greater than those in the surrounding region.

terms: Mesoscale
Scale of roughly 2 to 2000 km, between local and synoptic.
Gust front
Boundary of cold air outflow from a thunderstorm.
Derecho
Long-lived straight-line wind event associated with a fast-moving MCS.

questions.q: What is a gust front?
c: The leading edge of cold outflow from a thunderstorm
The warm inflow region feeding air into a mature supercell
The forward edge of the anvil cloud spreading ahead of a storm
A boundary where sea breeze air meets the land breeze at dawn
questions.e: Cold downdraft air spreads out at the surface and forms a gust front.

questions.q: How is a derecho best described?
c: A widespread, long-lived straight-line wind event
A single short-lived tornado with a narrow damage path
A tropical cyclone that has moved over cold water
A winter storm with blowing snow and low visibility
questions.e: Derechos produce damaging winds along a long swath, usually from a fast-moving MCS.

questions.q: What conditions cause lake-effect snow?
c: Cold air passes over relatively warm open water and becomes unstable
Warm moist air flows over a frozen lake and cools to saturation
A strong cold front stalls on land and lifts air over the shoreline
Calm high-pressure conditions allow lake fog to freeze onto the shore
questions.e: Heat and moisture from the lake destabilize the air and create intense snow bands on the lee shore.

questions.q: What is a squall line?
c: A line of thunderstorms with a gust front and shelf cloud
A narrow line of fog banks along a sea breeze front at dawn
A series of calm days between two passing warm fronts
A frontal wave visible as thin cirrus bands at high level
questions.e: Squall lines have organized lines of convection with a continuous gust front.

questions.q: A mesoscale convective complex (MCC) is mainly identified by:
c: A large, round cold cloud shield on infrared satellite imagery
A single funnel cloud descending from a rotating wall cloud
A hurricane-like eye with a clear centre on visible imagery
A halo around the sun produced by thin high ice cloud
questions.e: MCCs are defined by size and shape criteria on IR imagery.

questions.q: A squall line is:
c: A line of active thunderstorms, often ahead of a cold front
A single isolated storm cell with a very short life cycle
A tropical wave moving across the Atlantic in late summer
A sea breeze front that moves a few kilometres inland
questions.e: Squall lines are narrow bands of intense convection.

questions.q: A mesoscale convective complex is identified by:
c: Large, long-lived, near-circular cloud shield
A narrow plume of cloud from a single large thunderstorm
A single anvil that lasts for only about thirty minutes
A clear sky and light winds across a wide region
questions.e: An MCC has a cold cloud shield over a large area lasting many hours.

questions.q: What is a bow echo on radar?
c: A bow-shaped line of storms associated with damaging straight-line winds
A circular rain band spiralling around the centre of a hurricane
A hail signature showing large stones inside a single cell
A tornado hook echo at the rear flank of a supercell
questions.e: Bow echoes mark strong rear-inflow and wind damage.

questions.q: The gust front is:
c: The leading edge of outflow cooled by evaporation and downdrafts
The leading edge of the warm sector ahead of a cold front
A frontal occlusion where cold air overtakes the warm front
A high-level jet core on the polar side of the storm
questions.e: Storm outflow forms a mini cold front called a gust front.

questions.q: A cold pool beneath an MCS:
c: Helps trigger new convection along its leading edge
Prevents all new cells from forming near the system
Warms the surface and weakens the outflow boundary
Removes the shear and ends the organized convection
questions.e: The cold pool lifts warm air at its edge and sustains the system.

questions.q: Typical timescale of mesoscale systems is:
c: Hours to a day
Weeks
Seconds
Months
questions.e: Mesoscale phenomena last from a few hours up to about a day.

topics.title: Tropical cyclones and post-tropical transition
lesson: Tropical cyclones are warm-core, rotating storms that draw energy from warm ocean water. They threaten Atlantic Canada mostly in late summer and fall, usually in a weakened or transitioning state.

list: Sea surface temperature of about 26.5 C or warmer through a depth of about 50 m.
Weak vertical wind shear.
A pre-existing disturbance and a moist mid-troposphere.
Enough Coriolis effect, so generally at least 5 degrees from the equator.
Tropical depression: below 34 kt.
Tropical storm: 34 to 63 kt.
Hurricane: 64 kt (119 km/h) or more. Saffir-Simpson Category 1 starts here.

lesson: Atlantic hurricane season runs 1 June to 30 November, with the peak around mid-September. The Canadian Hurricane Centre, part of ECCC and based in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, forecasts tropical cyclone impacts for Canada.

Over cooler water (north of the Gulf Stream) and in stronger shear, a tropical cyclone loses its tropical structure. It develops fronts, a cold core, and a larger, asymmetric wind field. It is then called post-tropical. It can still be extremely dangerous. The wind field often expands, and rain and surge can remain high. Post-tropical Fiona (2022) caused severe damage in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.

lesson.note: 'Post-tropical' means the structure has changed, not that the hazard has gone.

terms: Warm core
Storm structure with the warmest air at the centre, typical of tropical cyclones.
Post-tropical
A cyclone that has lost its tropical characteristics but remains a significant storm.
Wind shear
Change in wind speed or direction with height.

questions.q: What is the minimum sea surface temperature generally needed for tropical cyclone development?
c: About 26.5 C
About 10 C
About 15 C
About 35 C
questions.e: Warm water (about 26.5 C or more to considerable depth) provides the heat and moisture.

questions.q: What sustained wind speed is the minimum for a hurricane?
c: 34 kt (63 km/h)
100 kt
50 kt
questions.e: Tropical storm becomes a hurricane at 64 kt sustained winds.

questions.q: What is the core structure of a tropical cyclone?
c: Warm core
Cold core
Frontal core
No defined core
questions.e: Latent heat release keeps the centre warm.

questions.q: What does 'post-tropical' mean?
c: The system has lost its tropical structure but can remain dangerous
The storm has dissipated and no longer poses any threat to land
The storm has weakened to a tropical depression over warm water
The storm has moved over land and its winds fall below gale force
questions.e: The storm has changed structure (often with fronts and a cold core) but may keep strong winds and heavy rain.

questions.q: When is the Atlantic hurricane season?
c: 1 June to 30 November
1 January to 30 June
1 September to 31 December
1 April to 31 July
questions.e: The official Atlantic season is June 1 to November 30.

questions.q: The Saffir-Simpson scale classifies hurricanes by:
c: Sustained wind speed
Central pressure only
Rainfall totals
Size
questions.e: Categories 1 to 5 are based on sustained winds.

questions.q: A hurricane in the Atlantic needs sea surface temperatures of at least about:
questions.e: Tropical cyclones need about 26.5 C or warmer water to develop.

questions.q: What happens when a hurricane moves over cold water or land?
c: It weakens due to lost heat and moisture supply
It strengthens, because the cold water adds fuel to the storm
It stays unchanged, since it is not tied to its energy source
It always speeds up and turns cold-core within the hour
questions.e: Warm water drives the storm; without it, the storm decays.

questions.q: Post-tropical transition means the system becomes:
c: Cold-core with frontal characteristics
Warm-core and smaller, with a more compact eye
A tornado-producing mesoscale convective system
A stationary front lying along the old storm track
questions.e: Transitioning storms acquire frontal structure and a cold core.

questions.q: In Canada, the Canadian Hurricane Centre is located in:
c: Dartmouth, Nova Scotia
Vancouver, British Columbia
Edmonton, Alberta
Gander, Newfoundland
questions.e: The CHC operates from the Atlantic Storm Prediction Centre in Dartmouth.

questions.q: The most dangerous part of a Northern Hemisphere hurricane is usually the:
c: Right-front quadrant
Left-rear quadrant
Left-front quadrant
The eye
questions.e: The right side adds forward motion to the rotational wind speed.
